messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam, a 56-year-old detective of Oceania background, came to treatment after years of carrying a childhood that still seemed to sit inside every shift and every quiet moment at home. He described being raised by a caregiver whose physical abuse was sudden, humiliating, and impossible to predict: the smell of something burnt in the kitchen would sometimes be the only warning before a blow, and even now that same acrid scent could pull him back without preparation to the cramped rooms, the heat, and the fear of waiting for what came next. He had learned to scan people quickly, especially those who looked like the men who had hurt him in childhood, and to mistrust even small flashes of warmth or ease. What unsettled him most was that positive emotion itself could feel dangerous, as if a rare moment of relief was the moment before something terrible happened. When he tried to talk about what had happened, he often lost the thread entirely and could not finish the story, and he would come away feeling that his own reactions proved he was a lousy coper and that there must be something fundamentally wrong with the kind of person he was. Over time, those beliefs had hardened into a conviction that the world did not operate by any rules he could trust; it had, in his words, “completely broken” the way he thought life was supposed to work.

Those meanings fed his memory in painful ways. When Liam tried to explain the abuse, the account would fragment, and the more he struggled to tell it in order, the more his mind would snap to vivid, uninvited scenes: a hand raised, the stale heat of the room, the burnt smell hanging in the air. The recollection was not distant or narrative in shape; it arrived with the force of something happening again, and with it came intense rage that made his jaw clench and his chest tighten. He said that the memory could be triggered instantly by something in his surroundings, as though his mind had learned to stand ready for a return of the old danger. At work, in the station or out on a scene, if he caught even a faint burnt odor from wiring, a kitchen fire, or scorched material, he would be thrown back into the abuse before he had time to think. If someone in the street or in a file photo resembled one of the victims he had seen over the years, he would feel the memory sharpen again, not only of the childhood assaults but of his own powerlessness in the face of them. His belief that his world had been shattered, and that he himself had somehow invited the treatment, kept the memories bound to shame and anger rather than history. The more he blamed himself, the more the scenes seemed to confirm that he had been weak all along, and the more he tried to explain, the less coherent the story became.

To manage this, Liam narrowed his life. He avoided other people whenever he could, ate lunch alone, and found reasons not to linger after work. He had even started avoiding clothes that resembled what he had worn at certain times in childhood, because the wrong shirt could make him feel exposed and stranded in an old role he hated. At the same time, pulling away from people and from the memories gave the recollections more room to intrude. When he detached himself from them, they returned less as something observed than as something that broke through abruptly, and that unpredictability made him even more alert. He remained superalert at home and on duty, having difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay watchful, and he noticed that his body reacted strongly whenever something reminded him of the abuse. He would jolt at small sounds, pace the house, and keep checking the door or the stove, as though the next threat might be waiting in the ordinary details of the room. That constant guardedness made it easier for the burnt smell, the sight of a similar face, or even a burst of unexpected happiness to catch him unprepared, and each fresh reminder seemed to confirm his conviction that the world could turn instantly. The more he withdrew and monitored for danger, the more isolated and self-critical he became, certain that these were the failures of a man who had not coped well enough and who could never quite keep himself safe.

By the time he sought help, the cycle had begun to cost him his marriage, his sleep, and his confidence at work. He was still functioning as a detective, but he was exhausted by the effort of staying on guard and frightened that one wrong smell or one unexpected moment of feeling good would throw him back into the old scenes in front of colleagues or suspects. What brought him in was the sense that the life he had built around vigilance was shrinking, and that he was becoming more cut off from everyone he cared about. He said he wanted relief, but what he feared most was that the memories would keep arriving without warning and prove, once again, that he was not someone who could ever truly withstand them.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows reminders leading to avoidance or hypervigilance, but it does not clearly state that triggers themselves drive Liam’s maladaptive strategies in a causal way within one paragraph.
The vignette states that a burnt smell and similar faces cue the memory, but it does not clearly present triggers as causing the traumatic memory in the required causal direction.
The vignette says self-blaming beliefs keep the memories bound to shame, but it does not explicitly show negative appraisals driving the traumatic memory itself in a causal sequence.
The vignette shows the memory being triggered by surroundings, but it does not explicitly state that the memory then leads to new triggers or increased triggering stimuli.
The vignette describes threat feelings increasing self-criticism, but it does not clearly show a sense of threat producing negative appraisals in the required causal relationship.
The vignette shows avoidance and monitoring making him more alert and vulnerable to reminders, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies cause the memory to recur in a causal way.
The vignette shows withdrawal increasing self-criticism, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals in the required causal relationship.
